did_you_know.text: The phrase “valuation of persons” does not mean that a person was sold; it means that someone making a vow promised a payment to the sanctuary, determined by age and sex.
“The sanctuary shekel” refers to an official weight standard, not necessarily to a particular coin. This made it possible to measure payments consistently.
The law takes the person’s financial situation into account: if the one making the vow cannot afford the regular amount, the priest may set a lower payment.
If an animal dedicated to God was exchanged for another animal, both were considered sacred. This prevented someone from replacing a better animal with an inferior one.
A “homer of barley” is a measure of the volume of seed, not of the land’s area. The field’s valuation was therefore linked to the amount of seed needed to sow it.
The value of a field dedicated after the Jubilee was calculated according to the number of years remaining until the next Jubilee. In other words, the remaining use of the field affected its price.
The Jubilee laws ensured that an ancestral field would not pass permanently from one person to another. In the Jubilee year, it returned to the family with the historic claim to it.
The verse explains that one shekel equals twenty gerahs. This shows that the Torah also defines the weight units used for sacred payments.

A “herem” is an absolute dedication, different from an ordinary dedication: it cannot be sold or redeemed with money. The term is connected with the idea of something being set apart completely for a sacred purpose.
The tithe here is one-tenth of agricultural produce, such as grain and fruit. This shows that the system of offerings included produce from the land, not only money or animals.

The tithe of cattle and sheep was counted as the herd passed one by one under a staff, and every tenth animal was dedicated. This prevented people from deliberately choosing which animals would be given.
